newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Alsace seen as test for Le Pen in French vote.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Alsace seen as test for Le Pen in French vote.

text.p: France's eastern border province of Alsace has low unemployment, little crime and relatively few immigrants, yet it gives extreme-rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen some of his best election scores.
Le Pen's openly xenophobic National Front chalks up its best results in the southeast where there is a high jobless rate and North African migrants even in the smallest villages.

But why does he win up to a third of the vote in some parts of Alsace, twice his national score, even though unemployment is among the lowest in France and there are few Arabs, although there is a sizeable Turkish minority in large towns?

Political scientists call it "Alsatian schizophrenia". They suspect the explanation may lie in the turbulent history which saw the province, which now has 1.7 million inhabitants, switch hands several times between France and Germany.
NATIONAL FRONT BENEFITS FROM PROTEST VOTE
As an outsider in French politics, the Front also benefits from protest votes from country-dwellers dissatisfied by the way society is going, they say.

"I'm voting for Le Pen's candidate because all the others, left or right, have just always lied to us," says shopowner Sylvie Lenz in the village of Barr, south of Strasbourg. "If Le Pen gets a lot of votes, perhaps those who run this country will pay attention to the middle class too.

"The government lets the rich get richer on the grounds that the country profits as a whole. The poor are protected by the all-encompassing welfare system. We in the middle are crippled by taxes and pay for everyone else," Lenz said.

Patriotism is also an issue. The Front's most vehement enemy in the area, Socialist Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautman said: "The National Front has abusively taken over the mantle of protector of French patriotism so dear to Alsatians."

Trained as a Protestant theologian, Trautman, 46, won national prominence, and Le Pen's enduring hatred, when she had the city's statue of national heroine Joan of Arc removed to prevent Le Pen staging a ceremony at its foot last month.
Trautman's leadership of anti-National Front activities when the party held its congress in Strasbourg in April has boosted her campaign for a parliamentary seat in the May 25-June 1 election.
She has become a hero in the picturesque streets of this thousand-year-old cathedral city of 400,000, official seat of the European Parliament and the Council of Europe.
"I suspect the business about the statue was part of her campaign to become national head of the Socialist party after the election," says Yvan Blot, the Front's leader in Alsace.
Blot, a defector from the ruling Gaullist party, is not standing against Trautman since the Front's scores in Strasbourg are only around the national average of 15 percent.
He is running instead in the nearby Saverne area, a region of forests and rolling farmlands dotted with half-timbered Hansel-and-Gretel-like villages.
FRONT APPEALS TO TRADITIONAL VALUES IN ALSACE
There are virtually no foreigners in most of the 162 villages in this constituency of 100,000 inhabitants, but the Front polled nearly 20 percent in the last general election in 1993.

"Immigration is a side issue here. What really counts is that people here believe in traditional values. The corruption of the ruling parties in the past years, both the Socialists and the centre-right, has shocked them terribly," said Blot, 48.
"People want respectability to become the norm again," the bespectacled, tweedy former senior civil servant said.
Blot's wing of the Front cultivates a suave image far from the aggressive extremism projected by some of the outspoken Le Pen's leather-jacketed, crop-haired supporters.

Extremism doesn't go down well in Alsace. Talking to voters in prosperous villages such as Singrist, Jetterswiller and Reutenburg, Blot tones down the Front's hard line and its vehement opposition to European unity, which is highly popular here.
Most residents took his leaflets politely, apparently impressed by a candidate who takes the trouble to canvass door-to-door in every village in his constituency.
Occasionally, one quickly closed the door on realising who the candidate was. Others told him: "We're with you."

"I learned this type of campaigning from (French President) Jacques Chirac when he was running for parliament in his rural constituency of Correze," said Blot, the only National Front leader who was a Gaullist parliamentarian before joining the extreme right.
Immigration does count to a degree although tensions seem milder than in other areas of France.
Most immigrants in Alsace are Turks, an overspill from the big immigrant community in Germany. They have been involved in some disputes over Moslem fundamentalism.

"If they want to become French, that's fine. We've integrated people from many countries. But if they want to live apart in closed communities, forcing their daughters to wear headscarves and perhaps veils tomorrow, that is not fine," said a restaurant owner in Bischwiller, an industrial town sometimes referred to as "Turkwiller" because of its Turkish minority.
"You can't imagine the amount of racism in this town," says a young American woman married to a local Frenchman. "The French hate the Turks and the Turks hate the French."
"They live completely separately," she said. "It's like different countries in the same town. Since both Turks and Alsatians are hard-headed and stubborn, I hate to think what will come of it."
